posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring CRO post with multiple ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain from a 'explainability' angle, positioning auditability as the real BI requirement, not AI avoidance
posts.draft_comment: The ban wasn't really about ChatGPT — it was about not being able to stand behind the output. That's a different problem than most AI vendors are solving for. The question I keep hearing from finance and risk teams isn't 'can AI analyse our data?' it's 'can we show our working to someone who has the power to fine us?' Those are very different products.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that it's not a training issue, leave her thinking
posts.draft_comment: The 18 months wasn't wasted on the wrong tool — it was spent on the wrong problem. People don't avoid dashboards because they're hard to use. They avoid them because the one time a number was wrong in a meeting, everyone remembered. What did your team do to rebuild that trust after the first bad data incident?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically just noise with a colour scheme. The thing I keep seeing is it's not even about the number of metrics — it's that most dashboards answer questions nobody actually asked. Someone built it to prove the data existed, not to help anyone decide anything. What made you land on those specific 5?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post about self-service BI chaos — validate the 'who owns the truth' pain with a sharper reframe, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so real — and honestly the number doesn't even matter, it's that each one becomes someone's personal source of truth. The tooling was never the problem. It's that 'self-service' quietly skipped the step where someone decides what revenue actually means before handing out licenses. Who owned that definition before the dashboards existed?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing hallucinations as security risk, with a CEO prospect watching — validate the framing, add the layer about trust being the real infrastructure problem
posts.draft_comment: The 'accuracy issue vs security issue' distinction is one more people need to hear. A hallucinated number that gets into a board deck or a compliance report doesn't announce itself — it just sits there looking credible. And the damage isn't just the bad decision, it's what happens to trust in the whole system after. How many orgs do you think are actually auditing AI-generated outputs the same way they'd audit a user upload?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm calling out BI vendor overpromise, with a COO prospect engaging — validate the core truth with a specific observation, then add the insight about who BI tools are actually designed for
posts.draft_comment: That £200k story is depressingly common. Most BI tools are designed to impress a procurement committee, not survive contact with a marketing manager on a Monday morning. The 'self-service' label usually means self-service for someone who already thinks in SQL. How many vendors have you seen actually test their product with a non-technical user before they ship it?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right' problem — validate the cultural root cause while adding the missing layer: culture needs a forcing mechanism, not just awareness
posts.draft_comment: The filter problem is almost never about the filters. It's that three teams had three slightly different questions and nobody agreed on what the single source of truth even was before they started clicking. Culture is the fix, yes — but culture needs a moment of friction to actually change, otherwise the next quarterly review looks exactly the same. What made the CFO ask this time rather than just quietly accepting the discrepancy?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the real adoption problem (nobody knows what to ask) — validate the 'blank page' insight and reframe shadow AI as a signal worth listening to
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is almost always a prompting problem, not a product problem. People know they need data but they don't know how to turn a business question into a query — and that gap doesn't close with training sessions. The ChatGPT-on-phones thing is actually the most honest feedback your vendor will never give you: what does it say about a tool when people prefer a workaround?
